newsitem.title: USA: Dole seeks upset on last night of campaign.
newsitem.headline: Dole seeks upset on last night of campaign.

text.p: Republican presidential candidate Bob Dole, his voice hoarse and prospects fading, limped into the final night of a marathon campaign push on Monday that he hoped would give him one of the great upsets in American history.

Dole was beginning his fourth consecutive night of around-the-clock campaigning, as part of a 96-hour, 19 state last ditch blitz to snatch victory for his flagging campaign in the waning hours before voting was to begin on Tuesday.
"We're going around the clock for America," Dole told a cheering rally in Lafayette, Louisiana. "We're going to continue without sleep, without rest to save America."
After speaking at the Vermilionville Living History Museum, Dole shrugged off the effects of non-stop campaigning and danced a Cajun two-step with his wife Elizabeth.
Dole's campaign was travelling with a limp. His campaign plane had a flat tire in Houston, before travelling to Lousiana.
Dole, his staff and the press corps that accompany him then commandeered the plane that carried the overflow press that regularly cannot cram onto the candidate's plane.
Confusion broke out on the tarmac as passenger lists were sorted out, frayed nerves came near to snapping and some travelers were forced to skip the Louisiana stop while the tire was fixed.
"Good omen. The press had a better plane all the time, and I didn't know it," Dole quipped aboard his temporary plane.
Dole addressed enthusiastic crowds in the thousands on Monday at stops in Arizona, New Mexico and Texas before arriving in Louisiana, but his voice was hoarse.

"I may not keep my voice but I will keep my word," Dole told about 3,000 cheering backers at a get-out-the-vote rally in Houston after being introduced by former President George Bush as a man of integrity.
Aides said Dole was taking something called "Throat Coat" -- a herbal tea made of slippery elm bark -- to soothe his voice from speech after speech at a pace of about one an hour.
Dole kept up his battering of Clinton over character and promised the Texans "I will not violate the public trust when I'm president of the United States."
"I have never known such arrogance in the White House ... as I've witnessed on almost a daily basis in the Clinton White House," he said.
"They say, 'Well we play be the rules.' They don't have any rules," said Dole. "They make up their own rules."
Before voting in his hometown of Russell, Kansas at noon on Tuesday, Dole will have touched down in Tennessee, Iowa and Missouri.

A Reuters/Zogby poll on Monday Clinton's lead over Dole had widened again after narrowing over the weekend. Clinton moved up to a 7.3 percentage point lead 44.2 to 36.9 percent with Perot at 7 percent and more than 10 percent undecided.
Dole has never been ahead of Clinton in polls which also show wide disinterest in this presidential election. But some polls have showed a narrowing under Dole's assault on ethics.

Aiming for a spectacular upset, Dole tells crowds which are modest compared Clinton's turnout that he is closing the campaign in the home town of the late Democratic President Harry Truman, who won an historic upset over Thomas Dewey in 1948.
"I may be the Harry Truman of 1996," he told radio talk show host Don Imus on Monday.
